Q: How do I extract the highest value in each list per key in a dictionary using for-loop? A:

Both of your loops are iterating the entire list. So the outer list outputs the "jumped at most" line, then the inner loop prints out all the maxes.

Just use another loop over items like you had to calculate the maxes:

for key, value in best.items():
    print(key, value)

Q: How can I yield list elements infinitely A:

You can use itertools.cycle. There's no need for another generator, just call cycle on an iterable, and it will cycle forever.

from itertools import cycle

for d in cycle(["dir_1", "dir_2", "dir_n"]):
    do stuff ...
    if some_reason:
        break

Q: Text Editor in C++ A:

Well, your requirements are the reason why students drop C++ and instead learn another language such as Python or Java -- these other students are not inundated with this nonsense. These silly restrictions of not being able to use even std::string is beyond ridiculous for a task such as creating a text editor.

The text editor is hard enough -- using container classes won't magically write the program for you -- you still have to put the program together.

Honestly, the requirements of not using even std::string, means to me that the project is really a C language project mixed in with maybe a few std::cout and new/delete calls, and not idiomatic C++.

Q: extracting particular numbers from a column of characters based on a criterion A:

We can use strcapture for this:

strcapture("([0-9]+) *: *([0-9]+)", col[[1]], list(year=0L, month=0L)) |>
  na.omit()
#     year month
# 8   1996     1
# 21  1997     1
# 34  1998     1
# 47  1999     1
# 60  2000     1
# 73  2001     1
# 86  2002     1
# 99  2003     1
# 112 2004     1
# 125 2005     1
# 138 2006     1
# 151 2007     1
# 164 2008     1
# 177 2009     1
# 190 2010     1
# 203 2011     1
# 216 2012     1
# 229 2013     1
# 242 2014     1
# 255 2015     1
# 268 2016     1
# 281 2017     1
# 294 2018     1
# 307 2019     1
# 320 2020     1
# 333 2021     1
# 346 2022     1
# 359 2023     1
# 372 2024     1
# 385 2025     1
# 398 2026     1

Since you want to keep the non-year months as well, then

library(dplyr)
col |>
  filter(grepl("[0-9]", `...1`)) |>
  mutate(
    y = if_else(grepl(":", `...1`), trimws(sub(":.*", "", `...1`)), NA),
    m = trimws(if_else(grepl(":", `...1`), sub(".*:", "", `...1`), `...1`))
  )
# # A tibble: 361 × 3
#    ...1      y     m    
#    <chr>     <chr> <chr>
#  1 1996 :  1 1996  1    
#  2 2         <NA>  2    
#  3 3         <NA>  3    
#  4 4         <NA>  4    
#  5 5         <NA>  5    
#  6 6         <NA>  6    
#  7 7         <NA>  7    
#  8 8         <NA>  8    
#  9 9         <NA>  9    
# 10 10        <NA>  10   
# # ℹ 351 more rows
# # ℹ Use `print(n = ...)` to see more rows

And if you want to include a portion from a previous question, then add |> fill(year) to the end :-)

(I used dplyr in that second code block, but it can easily be done in base R if desired.)

For the "last", we can add some more code,

dat <- col |>
  filter(grepl("[0-9]", `...1`)) |>
  mutate(
    y = if_else(grepl(":", `...1`), trimws(sub(":.*", "", `...1`)), NA),
    m = trimws(if_else(grepl(":", `...1`), sub(".*:", "", `...1`), `...1`)),
    across(c(y, m), ~ as.integer(.x))
  ) |>
  fill(y)

The last year and last year/month:

slice_max(dat, order_by = data.frame(y, m))
# # A tibble: 1 × 3
#   ...1          y     m
#   <chr>     <int> <int>
# 1 2026 :  1  2026     1

If you want the last month of each year,

slice_max(dat, by = y, order_by = m)
# # A tibble: 31 × 3
#    ...1      y     m
#    <chr> <int> <int>

Q: Get start / end row when value changes A:

Here is the solution with LAG. First get the previous rank for each row. Then only keep the rows you are interested in (switch to 5 or switch from 5).

Then, I simply number these rows 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, etc. and integer-divide these row numbers by 2, so as to get group numbers 0, 1, 2, etc. For each group, the first date is the added date and the later date is the removed date.

with
  series as
  (
    select 
      ticker, rank, dt,
      lag(rank) over (partition by ticker order by dt) as prev_rank 
    from mytable
  ),
  grouped as
  (
    select
      ticker, dt,
      trunc((row_number() over (partition by ticker order by dt) - 1) / 2) as grp
    from series
    where (rank = 5 and (prev_rank <> 5 or prev_rank is null))
       or (rank <> 5 and prev_rank = 5)
  )
select ticker, min(dt) as added, max(dt) as removed
from grouped
group by ticker, grp
order by ticker, grp;

Demo: https://dbfiddle.uk/tpMm15jx

Q: How can I use Symfony AssetMapper with npm packages installed in the root node_modules? A:

When using Symfony AssetMapper with npm packages, you can keep all npm packages in root /node_modules and selectively register the subfolders containing the package entry points for AssetMapper.

Workflow example:

1️⃣ Register the folders in AssetMapper

bin/console assets:register node_modules/@hpcc-js/wasm/dist/

2️⃣ Require the package in importmap

bin/console importmap:require @hpcc-js/wasm --path=./node_modules/@hpcc-js/wasm/dist/index.js
  • This creates a mapping in the importmap that tells the browser where to find @hpcc-js/wasm.

3️⃣ Clear Symfony cache

bin/console cache:clear

4️⃣ Use the package in the browser

import { Graphviz } from "@hpcc-js/wasm";

const gv = new Graphviz();
gv.layout("digraph { a -> b }", "svg").then(svg => {
  document.body.innerHTML = svg;
});

Key points:

  • Only the registered folders are served by AssetMapper.
  • All relative imports inside the registered folders work automatically.
  • Root node_modules is still available for Node/Vite tooling.
  • Registered folders must include all dependencies that the package imports in the browser.

5️⃣ Alternative approach

Some users create a postinstall script in package.json to copy necessary files from root node_modules into assets/vendor, for example:

"postinstall": "cp -R node_modules/@organization assets/vendor/@organization"

This can be useful if you want to expose only specific files instead of an entire folder. However, it duplicates files and requires maintenance whenever packages are updated. Note that not everything in a registered folder is necessarily compiled into the public build; AssetMapper only compiles and serves the files in the registered folders that are needed for browser imports.

In most cases — including @hccp-js/wasm, where the entire dist directory is intended for the browser — registering the relevant folder with AssetMapper is cleaner, avoids duplication, and automatically resolves relative imports.

Reference: For more details and discussion, see the Symfony issue: https://github.com/symfony/symfony-docs/issues/22000
